summary: Replace 60/130 with the verse containing the women under the rope.
rationale: The supplied PrS 57/36 has the same clause Kmičoki an niše ayna d lə kməṭʕono taḥt u šəriṭo and the same context of women unable to become pregnant stepping under a rope. summary: Restore the first-person plural possessive on our cook.

summary: Use the feminine article before mare.

summary: The aggregate counts corroborate frequent literal I carrying, III loading and I Detransitive pregnancy; they do not require additional occurrence decisions. Existing active and Detransitive numbering is not parallel and is retained.

III loading alternates between a cargo object with an ʕal-marked carrier and a pack-animal/equipment object with cargo expressed separately. Hors 2/31 additionally has a beneficiary suffix. Human load-bearers occur in MAC NE Famine/68. This is valency variation within III.1.

I Detransitive pregnancy includes becoming pregnant and the resulting state, with animal as well as human subjects. PrS 1/2 has m- identifying the father; it is not an expressed loading agent. Animal pregnancy is already covered by trächtig in the inherited gloss.

The forms ṭʕino and ṭʕine must not be filed by English tense wording alone. PrS 60/10 ṭʕino is retained with the finite pregnancy paradigm, whereas plural ṭʕine predicates pregnancy states. The productive agent noun ṭaʕono is not evidence for a Part act. box.

Existing ġamo and ruḥo idioms explain the worry and setting-out tokens; no additional numbered senses are needed. Their new contextual attestations are recorded in decisions without duplicating the idiom list.

51/9 and 51/24 present a carrying riddle; 51/10 explicitly reflects a literal interpretation. The supplied verses do not themselves give the alleged explanation at 51/26, so a lexical storytelling sense is withheld.

Existing III Detransitive Part. Pass. examples already attest loaded mules/rafts and EL 36 = Hors 1/36. No new label is imposed on this unnumbered section. PrS 10/69 and 31/9 support the same resultant loaded state.

Verify the supplied PrS verse numbers against the inherited page/line references (PrS 1/2 versus prs 1/3; PrS 57/36 versus prs 153/31; PrS 80/76 versus prs 234/15; PrS 84/17 versus prs 244/24). Identical sentences are withheld rather than recited under competing references.

Confirm whether PrS 48/16 ṭʕenunne and PrS 84/17 Ṭʕalli have reduced III a-/ma- or are I Imperativ forms. Their loading meaning alone does not establish III; the inherited aṭʕal-li cannot be silently substituted for supplied Ṭʕalli.
Confirm ṭʕinile in JTM 4.4/15 as active Preterit with a plural object and l-marked agent, and person/object segmentation of gəṭuʕannən in 4.4/14.
Compare feminine ṭʕino and Ṭuʕnono with ṭʕənto; confirm event/state contrast without replacing the source vocalism.
95/17 and 113/201 carry alignment warnings. Their supplied translations are not quoted; check the final negation in 95/17 and carrier/patient relation and -walla in 113/201.
54/75 has an Infinitiv token but the supplied German stops before the target clause; recover the matching edition translation before using this example.
Check 51/26 directly before treating the carrying riddle as a conventional figurative use. Is the eye-subject intolerance pattern conventional, and how does l ʕaynayye agree in 95/63?
Is initial t in 60/84 tʕəlle an edition typo? No correction of the existing entry is supported by that uncorrected token.
Correct läd er → lädt er.
rationale: The third-person singular of laden is lädt. The missing final t remains a typo even though the supplied edition translation repeats it.

summary: Correct began er → begann er.
rationale: The German past tense of beginnen is begann. The span occurs in the translation of the 21/55 example in idiom ṭʕn-1.idiom.2.

summary: Correct the capitalization in eine schwere Last.
rationale: In the 29/38 translation in idiom ṭʕn-1.idiom.2, schwere is an attributive adjective and Last is the noun. Their capitalization is reversed.

summary: Unmoving bones, arches, timber and stones bear loads; physical support requires no distinct lexical sense.

Eyes and conscience stand for the experiencer of inability to tolerate a situation. Clausal stimuli and postverbal l-marked experiencers occur alongside simple nominal objects; fixed envy idiom status is unproved.
